title: Masquerading: Double File Extension
summary: Double file extension masquerading exploits the gap between the file name a user sees and the extension the operating system acts on. A name such as a document suffix followed by an executable suffix is handled by the final extension, yet file browsers and mail clients that hide known extensions render only the first one, so the item appears to be a document. The technique is a delivery and user execution enabler rather than a persistence mechanism, and it is common in spearphishing attachments and in archive contents. Detection benefits from looking at the complete file name with extensions shown, from counting dots and identifying the effective extension, and from treating the combination as an indicator in itself when the first extension belongs to an inert type. Windows also records a separate type field for registered file types, and email gateways rewrite or strip dangerous attachment extensions, so defenders should combine name analysis with file header inspection and with process creation records showing an office or archive application spawning a script interpreter or shell.

beginner.definition: This is a trick that uses two file extensions in one file name, such as a text file name ending with a program extension. Many programs on your computer hide the real extension. You see only the harmless first one. When you open the file, the last extension decides what runs.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most people trust the extension they can see. If it says text or image, they open the file without worry. The hidden second extension means the file is actually a program. This trick often arrives as an email attachment. It turns a normal user action into an infection.
howItWorks: The attacker builds a malicious program and saves it with two extensions.
The first extension looks harmless, such as text, document or image.
The second extension is a program type, such as an executable or a script.
The operating system decides how to open the file from the last extension.
Many file listings hide known extensions and show only the harmless first one.
The user opens what looks like a document and the program runs instead.
beginner.example: Think of a parcel wrapped in two layers. The outside wrapper says soft clothes, which looks harmless at the sorting desk. Underneath, the inner wrapper says fragile glass. The desk acts on the inner label and moves it very carefully, while the outside label fooled the clerk.
takeaways: Turn on the option that shows full file extensions in your file browser.
A file name with two extensions is unusual and deserves extra care.
Check the real file type from its contents, not from its name.

objectives: Explain how a double extension produces a misleading displayed name.
Describe which extension decides how a file is opened.
Explain how this sub-technique supports user execution and initial access.
Identify the settings and tools that reveal full file extensions.
Describe how to confirm a file's true type from its content.
